sentences.text: Although morphologically similar to modern hummingbirds, this extinct bird retained primitive features and is not closely related to any specific living species.
Specimens are among the smallest fossil birds and are classified in the order Apodiformes due to their shortened humeri and ulnae.
In some species, the skull and beak have been measured to be approximately 34 millimeters in length.
The beaks are straight and narrow, measuring 15.5 to 20 millimeters in length, which is roughly 2.5 times the length of the cranium.
The ulna measures between 6.7 and 8.8 millimeters, which is shorter than the 13-millimeter ulna found in Jungornis.
The humeri measure between 6.0 and 6.5 millimeters and are considered short and stout compared to other Apodiformes, except extant hummingbirds.
Elongated beaks, a feature unknown in Jungornis, serve as evidence of their ability to consume nectar.
Widely separated maxillary processes in the palatine bones indicate that the animal possessed rhynchokinesis, the ability to flex the upper beak.
Large hyoid bones are thought to have supported a long, protractile tongue used for lapping up nectar.
The genus Eurotrochilus was described by Gerald Mayr in 2004.
Dr. Gerald Mayr first described the extinct bird after finding tiny skeletons in museum drawers.
Two species are currently recognized: E. inexpectatus described by Mayr in 2004 and E. noniewiczi described by Bochenski in 2007.
The species E. noniewiczi is named after Edward Noniewicza, the private collector who discovered the fossil specimen.
Six specimens of Eurotrochilus have been found across Germany, France, and Poland.
Dr. Antoine Louchart described a French specimen in 2007, which included an almost complete skeleton preserved on a slab.
The Polish specimen found at Winnica serves as the holotype for the new species Eurotrochilus noniewiczi.
Adaptations allowed it to consume nectar from ornithophilous flowers as its main nutrient source and to pollinate those flowers.
Specializations in the humeri allowed the bone to rotate during hovering flight.
The warm climate supported broad-leaved evergreen forests and palm-rich coastal forests where the bird lived.
Scientists believe Eurotrochilus experienced mild winters based on its fruit and nectar diet, though migration habits are unknown.
Researchers suggest that Old World bird-pollinated flowers evolved their specific shapes in response to the bird, which had long beaks, tongues, and hovering flight.
The abundance of E. inexpectatus fossils suggests these birds were locally dominant pollinators of ornithophilous flowers in the early Oligocene.
Eurotrochilus is an extinct genus of stem-group hummingbirds and represents the closest known relatives to the crown group Trochilidae.
Eurotrochilus provided the strongest evidence that modern-looking hummingbirds existed in the Old World during the early Oligocene.
Eurotrochilus belongs to the family Trochilidae.
Eurotrochilus lived during the Rupelian age of the Early Oligocene epoch within the Paleogene period.
Specimens of Eurotrochilus date to between 28 and 34 million years ago, with German fossils estimated at 32 million years old.
During the Oligocene, the Paratethys Ocean covered most of Central and Eastern Europe where Eurotrochilus fossils were found.
It is debated whether competition with long-tongued bees caused the extinction of Eurotrochilus and European hummingbirds.
Rapid climate change is another hypothesis for the extinction of Eurotrochilus, which would have been difficult for such a small bird to survive.
